item.title: Why dont we use probability directly as loss func like 1-p or 1_by_p ?
item.description:
Why dont we use probability directly as loss func like 1-p or 1/p

Using raw probabilities like L=1−pL = 1 - pL=1−p or L=1/pL = 1/pL=1/p instead of −log⁡(p)-\log(p)−log(p) breaks down during gradient descent due to gradient saturation, information-theoretic inconsistency, and exponential vanishing in joint probabilities.

1. The Gradient Vanishing Problem (1−p1 - p1−p)

In neural networks, the probability ppp is obtained by passing raw logits zzz through an activation function like Softmax or Sigmoid.

Consider a single binary output where p=σ(z)=11+e−zp = \sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}p=σ(z)=1+e−z1​. The derivative of the sigmoid is:

∂p∂z=p(1−p) \frac{\partial p}{\partial z} = p(1 - p) ∂z∂p​=p(1−p)

Now evaluate the gradient of loss with respect to the logit zzz for both functions:

Under Linear Loss L=1−pL = 1 - pL=1−p:

∂L∂z=∂L∂p⋅∂p∂z=(−1)⋅p(1−p)=p2−p \frac{\partial L}{\partial z} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial p} \cdot \frac{\partial p}{\partial z} = (-1) \cdot p(1 - p) = p^2 - p ∂z∂L​=∂p∂L​⋅∂z∂p​=(−1)⋅p(1−p)=p2−p
  • When the model is completely wrong (z≪0  ⟹  p≈0z \ll 0 \implies p \approx 0z≪0⟹p≈0): ∂L∂z≈0 \frac{\partial L}{\partial z} \approx 0 ∂z∂L​≈0
  • Result: The gradient vanishes. When the model makes a confident, catastrophic error, the learning signal drops to zero, and the network cannot update its weights to escape the bad state.

Under Cross-Entropy Loss L=−log⁡(p)L = -\log(p)L=−log(p):

∂L∂z=∂L∂p⋅∂p∂z=(−1p)⋅p(1−p)=−(1−p)=p−1 \frac{\partial L}{\partial z} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial p} \cdot \frac{\partial p}{\partial z} = \left(-\frac{1}{p}\right) \cdot p(1 - p) = -(1 - p) = p - 1 ∂z∂L​=∂p∂L​⋅∂z∂p​=(−p1​)⋅p(1−p)=−(1−p)=p−1
  • When the model is completely wrong (p≈0p \approx 0p≈0): ∂L∂z≈−1 \frac{\partial L}{\partial z} \approx -1 ∂z∂L​≈−1
  • Result: The log cancels out the activation’s squashing derivative. The gradient is strictly proportional to the error (p−y)(p - y)(p−y), delivering a constant, healthy gradient update regardless of how wrong the network is.

2. The Instability and Curvature Problem (1/p1/p1/p)

If we choose L=1pL = \frac{1}{p}L=p1​, the loss function scales inversely with probability:

∂L∂p=−1p2 \frac{\partial L}{\partial p} = -\frac{1}{p^2} ∂p∂L​=−p21​∂L∂z=(−1p2)⋅p(1−p)=−1−pp=1−1p \frac{\partial L}{\partial z} = \left(-\frac{1}{p^2}\right) \cdot p(1 - p) = -\frac{1 - p}{p} = 1 - \frac{1}{p} ∂z∂L​=(−p21​)⋅p(1−p)=−p1−p​=1−p1​
  • When p→0p \to 0p→0: ∂L∂z→−∞\frac{\partial L}{\partial z} \to -\infty∂z∂L​→−∞.
  • The issue: The gradient diverges as a hyperbola (O(1/p)O(1/p)O(1/p)) rather than the smooth linear error (p−1)(p - 1)(p−1) of cross-entropy.
  • A single out-of-distribution token or misclassified edge case causes an immediate gradient explosion, blowing up the optimizer’s momentum buffers (Adam’s first and second moments) and corrupting the weight tensors.

3. Joint Probabilities and Sequence Likelihoods

In language models, the objective is to maximize the joint probability of a sequence of tokens W=(w1,w2,…,wT)W = (w_1, w_2, \dots, w_T)W=(w1​,w2​,…,wT​):

P(W)=∏t=1TP(wt∣w<t) P(W) = \prod_{t=1}^T P(w_t \mid w_{\lt t}) P(W)=t=1∏T​P(wt​∣w<t​)

Why linear loss fails on sequences:

If you define the sequence loss linearly:

L=1−P(W)=1−∏t=1Tpt L = 1 - P(W) = 1 - \prod_{t=1}^T p_t L=1−P(W)=1−t=1∏T​pt​
  • For a moderate sequence of 512 tokens, even if each token has high probability (pt≈0.99p_t \approx 0.99pt​≈0.99): ∏t=15120.99≈0.0057  ⟹  L≈0.9943 \prod_{t=1}^{512} 0.99 \approx 0.0057 \implies L \approx 0.9943 t=1∏512​0.99≈0.0057⟹L≈0.9943
  • For lower probabilities (pt≈0.5p_t \approx 0.5pt​≈0.5): ∏t=15120.5≈10−154 \prod_{t=1}^{512} 0.5 \approx 10^{-154} t=1∏512​0.5≈10−154
  • Under standard floating-point representation (float32 or bfloat16), this leads to immediate arithmetic underflow to zero, rendering computation impossible.

Why the logarithm is required:

Applying −log⁡-\log−log converts the product into an additive sum:

LNLL=−log⁡P(W)=−∑t=1Tlog⁡P(wt∣w<t) L_{\text{NLL}} = -\log P(W) = -\sum_{t=1}^T \log P(w_t \mid w_{\lt t}) LNLL​=−logP(W)=−t=1∑T​logP(wt​∣w<t​)
  • Multiplication becomes addition, preventing numerical underflow.
  • The total loss decomposes cleanly into token-level losses, allowing gradients to be computed and backpropagated independently to each token position: ∂L∂zt=pt−1 \frac{\partial L}{\partial z_t} = p_t - 1 ∂zt​∂L​=pt​−1

4. Maximum Likelihood and Information Theory

  • Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE): Minimizing −log⁡(p)-\log(p)−log(p) is mathematically equivalent to maximizing the log-likelihood of the data distribution under the model parameters: arg⁡max⁡θ∑ilog⁡Pθ(yi∣xi)≡arg⁡min⁡θ∑i−log⁡Pθ(yi∣xi) \arg\max_\theta \sum_i \log P_\theta(y_i \mid x_i) \equiv \arg\min_\theta \sum_i -\log P_\theta(y_i \mid x_i) argθmax​i∑​logPθ​(yi​∣xi​)≡argθmin​i∑​−logPθ​(yi​∣xi​)
  • Surprisal / Self-Information: In information theory, the information content of an event is I(p)=log⁡2(1/p)=−log⁡2(p)I(p) = \log_2(1/p) = -\log_2(p)I(p)=log2​(1/p)=−log2​(p). An event with p=1p=1p=1 carries 000 bits of surprise, whereas an event with p→0p \to 0p→0 carries infinite surprise. Cross-entropy directly minimizes the average bit surprise (entropy) of the true labels under the predicted model distribution. Neither 1−p1-p1−p nor 1/p1/p1/p corresponds to a valid metric of information divergence.
